synopsis: Photogrammetry, laser scanning and SLAM measure real sites from photographs, laser distances and machine recordings respectively; reality capture is strongest for preserving real geometry and clutter, but does not automatically yield simulation-ready truth [f13133, f3701, f5104]. The booklet recommends parameterised representative site types anchored to surveyed real sites; a possible starting portfolio of 15–30 archetypes and 3–5 lidar-plus-photogrammetry anchors is explicitly a planning assumption, not an evidence-based target [f3705, f4112]. Accuracy claims need reconciliation: survey capture is described as assessable against standards, while some passages restrict that distinction to laser scanning, despite ASPRS 2024 covering photogrammetry and a separate finding reporting controlled photogrammetric centimetre-level accuracy; the cited lidar result of 1.3 cm mean absolute error concerns road scenes [f78, f13136, f3719, f4198, f3721]. Photogrammetry is vulnerable to textureless soil, glare, motion and baked lighting, while forward-facing machine logs leave unseen surfaces that a taller future sensor may expose [f3722, f3873, f3811, f3812]. For the 2027 schedule, reconstruction-quality logs should be collected before sensor selection, with synchronised timestamps and retained calibration; adverse-weather replay should be separated from clean static-site mapping, although no off-road study was found quantifying weather contamination of reconstructed geometry [f4059, f4016, f4043, f4044]. Closed-loop braking requires substantial conversion beyond reconstruction, and captured moving objects need replacement with controllable agents; reusable site representation remains a bottleneck before scenario volume matters [f4000, f3885, f9364].
